tier_reason: The arena harness is public (sofa-buffers/arena languages/c-embedded/setup.sh, protobuf/bench.c, nanopb/bench.c) and the figures match its README and results/RESULTS.txt, but the host CPU and compiler version are not stated and protobuf-c's runtime is a prebuilt distro library with unstated version and flags, so not A; the arena is a little-known rival-codec harness, not a well-known suite, so not B. The older pbtools benchmark (gcc 8.3.0, i7-4510U, flags per row) points the same way but drives nanopb through its slow callback API and mixes runs, so it does not lift the tier.

corrections.workload: Encode plus decode of one 494-byte protobuf message (all scalar widths, floats, strings, bytes, eight numeric arrays, a nested struct, an array of structs, Unicode strings) in the arena's c-embedded host target (languages/c-embedded). Each timed iteration packs the same statically built message into a preallocated buffer and then unpacks it: protobuf-c mallocs the decoded tree and frees it every iteration, and nanopb decodes into a memset stack struct with fixed-size fields set in nanopb/message.options. 500,000 iterations by default (bench.sh), best of 5 runs with a 10 s cooldown between runs.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Arena 'Embedded - throughput' table: protobuf-c 328.0 MB/s (663,929 msg/s) vs nanopb 61.9 MB/s (125,240 msg/s), about 5.3x on both metrics (derived from page data). Older corroboration in the pbtools benchmark (eerimoq/pbtools benchmark/README.rst, gcc 8.3.0, Intel Core i7-4510U): encoding protobuf-c -O3 1.892 s vs nanopb -O2 9.580 s (about 5.1x) and decoding 2.508 s vs 6.433 s (about 2.6x) (derived from page data), with nanopb driven through its callback API. In the same pbtools table protobuf-c encodes faster than Google protobuf C++ 3.6.1 at -O3 (1.892 s vs 2.231 s, about 1.18x) but decodes slower (2.508 s vs 1.997 s, about 0.80x) (derived from page data). No msgpack comparison found.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc from the arena's Ubuntu 26.04 devcontainer (version not stated). The bench driver and the generated code are built with -Os -flto -std=c99 (languages/c-embedded/setup.sh). nanopb's runtime (git tag 0.4.9.1) is compiled from source at -Os -flto, but protobuf-c is linked with -lprotobuf-c against the distro's prebuilt libprotobuf-c (libprotobuf-c-dev), so the protobuf-c runtime's version and build flags are not stated and are not -Os.
corrections.caveats: Third-party numbers from a rival codec's benchmark arena (SofaBuffers, 0 stars) in which protobuf-c and nanopb are both baselines of the 'Embedded' throughput table, where speed is explicitly not the ranking metric. Host CPU and compiler version are not stated, so the run is not reproducible as published (the harness code is public). The build is asymmetric in protobuf-c's favour: every codec's bench driver and generated code are built -Os -flto and nanopb's runtime is compiled from source at -Os -flto, but protobuf-c's runtime is the distro's prebuilt libprotobuf-c linked with -lprotobuf-c, so its hot code runs at the distro's (unstated) flags; pbtools' own rows put nanopb at -Os about 1.35x (encode) to 1.5x (decode) slower than at -O2 (derived from page data). The c-embedded loops re-encode the original static message every iteration, not the freshly decoded one as the arena README describes for its maxspeed targets. One message shape, one unnamed host, and the 5.3x ratio compares two rows of one table. The older pbtools benchmark corroborates the direction but drives nanopb through its callback API (strings and sub-messages via pb_encode_string and pb_encode_submessage callbacks), mixes runs (protobuf-c -O3 rows from September 2019, nanopb -O2 rows re-run in January 2020 after commit 6000b5f switched common.mk to -O2), statically links an unstated libprotobuf-c version, and shows protobuf-c decoding about 1.26x slower than Google protobuf C++ 3.6.1 (derived from page data). The GLD.SerializerBenchmark C suite also lists protobuf-c, but according to the search record its protobuf-c row times a shared in-tree proto3 wire codec rather than protobuf-c itself (not re-checked by the verifier), so it was not used. No benchmark or performance numbers exist in the protobuf-c README. Last commit 2025-04-07 (release 1.5.2); the GLD suite author opened a benchmark-fairness review request (#803, 2026-07-17) and a spec-compliance report for 1.5.2 (#810, 2026-09-14), both still open.

notes: Arena numbers verified exactly (328.0 vs 61.9 MB/s, 663,929 vs 125,240 msg/s; 5.30x derived). Shortcomings to record: CPU and compiler version unstated, rival-codec arena, nanopb runtime built -Os -flto from source while protobuf-c uses the prebuilt distro library, static message re-encoded rather than the decoded one, one message shape; pbtools corroborates about 5x encode and 2.6x decode vs nanopb but with nanopb on callbacks, and there protobuf-c decodes slower than Google protobuf C++ 3.6.1. Metadata confirmed (BSD-2-Clause, 3.0k stars, last commit 2025-04-07, stale); not a duplicate, though pbtools (wave 1, tier A) already uses protobuf-c as a baseline.

tier_reason: PR #53's 'Before' table holds all six figures and the harness (test/benchmark/main.cpp, Google Benchmark) is public, but the post gives only 'Release mode': no CPU, compiler, flags or protobuf version. It is the project's own benchmark run by a contributor, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated beyond 'Release mode': the PR author introduces the tables as 'Here is a benchmarks (in Release mode)'; compiler, version, exact flags, CPU and protobuf version are not given. test/benchmark/CMakeLists.txt prints '[TIP] Release mode is expected in benchmark test'.
corrections.caveats: Numbers come from a contributor's (basiliscos) pull-request description (PR #53, opened 2025-07-08, still open) and not from the README, docs or CI. The PR says only that the runs were 'in Release mode' and omits CPU, compiler, flags and the protobuf version. The harness source is public (test/benchmark/main.cpp), so a rerun is possible, but the published figures are not fully specified. The same PR's decode optimization (145 ns unsafe, 162 ns safe) is unmerged, and review found a length-counting bug in it (it decremented an item count instead of a byte count), so only the 'Before' figures are used. Harness flaws: the encode loops pass neither the output buffer to DoNotOptimize nor call ClobberMemory, so stores from the header-only, fully inlined protopuf encoder could be eliminated, while protobuf's SerializeToArray is an out-of-line library call that also runs ByteSizeLong first. Both decoders are handed the whole 64-byte array (45 wire bytes plus 19 zero bytes) and neither result is checked; since tag 0 is invalid in protobuf, ParseFromArray should end with an error after parsing the real data. The message is tiny (45 bytes, all strings within small-string length), and both decode loops construct a fresh message per iteration (protobuf without an Arena). The unsafe_mode rows skip bounds checks, so the headline 4.0x encode ratio is with checks off; safe_mode gives 2.3x on encode and only 1.12x on decode. The README has no benchmark section, and the protopuf.surge.sh docs were not reachable (EGRESS_BLOCKED in the search session).

notes: All six 'Before' figures and the derived ratios (encode 4.0x unsafe and 2.3x safe, decode 1.30x and 1.12x) match the PR. Shortcomings to record: environment unspecified beyond Release mode, numbers from an unmerged PR whose 'After' optimization has a bug, encode output not protected by DoNotOptimize, both decoders given a zero-padded 64-byte buffer with results unchecked, tiny message, and the headline uses unsafe_mode. Metadata confirmed (Apache-2.0, 207 stars, last commit 2026-10-02, vcpkg and Conan Center badges); no duplicate found.
